opus-5.5.text:
I think Meta's move last year was a real shock to the market. Before that, compensation for top AI researchers was already high, but it followed a familiar pattern: a strong base salary, equity, and some negotiation room if you had a competing offer. When Meta started making offers in the tens of millions, and for a few people reportedly far beyond that, it reset everyone's sense of what a top researcher is "worth."

The first effect was psychological. Suddenly everyone in the field was asking, "What's my number?" Even people who had no plans to leave started wondering whether they were underpaid. Other companies had to respond, with retention packages, accelerated vesting, and counteroffers, so the price went up across the board, not just for the people Meta actually hired.

But I think it's important to separate the very top tier from the broader market. Meta was paying for a small number of people who had built frontier models, people who knew the full recipe for pretraining, post-training, infrastructure, and scaling. That talent is genuinely scarce. Maybe a few hundred people in the world have that end-to-end experience. For them, the price became almost like an athlete's or a star CEO's. For the average ML engineer, the effect was much smaller.

From Meta's point of view, I can understand the logic. If you believe AI is the most important technology of the next decade and you're behind, then spending a few billion dollars on people is small compared with what you're spending on GPUs and data centers. Compute costs tens of billions. If the right team can make that compute twice as effective, the talent is actually cheap.

What I'm less sure about is whether money alone builds a great team. Research culture matters a lot. The people who do breakthrough work are usually motivated by the problem, by their colleagues, and by having the freedom to try ambitious things. If you assemble a group of stars primarily with money, you still have to make them work together, agree on a direction, and stay patient when things don't work right away. That's the harder part, and we'll only know in a few years whether it worked.

For robotics, which is my area, the impact has been more indirect. The money was concentrated on large language model people. But it raised the overall temperature. Robotics researchers who understand foundation models are now much more sought after, and many startups are raising big rounds and competing for the same people. So I'd say Meta set off a chain reaction. It didn't just change one company's hiring; it changed how the whole industry thinks about the value of AI talent.

r001.rationale: The response describes a very small pool of top researchers and says other companies had to compete with retention packages and counteroffers, communicating high demand against limited supply.

r002.rationale: It says compute costs tens of billions and that a team making compute twice as effective makes talent cheap, presenting high compensation as economically justified by better use of expensive compute.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare high compensation with acquiring companies to obtain similar talent.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Meta's impact has been huge, and honestly it's reshaped the whole market in a very short time.

Before this summer, the compensation for top AI researchers was already high by any normal standard, but it was still within a range that people understood. Then Meta started building the superintelligence lab, and Zuckerberg personally went out recruiting. The numbers that came out, tens of millions a year, in some cases packages that were reported at over a hundred million over several years, were on a completely different scale. Whether every single reported number is accurate or not, the effect is the same: it reset everyone's anchor for what a top researcher is "worth."

I'd break the impact into a few layers.

The first layer is the very top, maybe a few dozen people in the world. These are the people who have actually trained frontier models end to end, who know where the bodies are buried, so to speak. For them, Meta basically turned the hiring market into something that looks more like professional sports. You have a franchise owner with essentially unlimited budget who has decided that this is the thing he's willing to spend on, and when one buyer behaves that way, every other team has to respond. OpenAI, Google, Anthropic all had to think about retention in a way they didn't before. I've heard from friends that people who had no intention of leaving suddenly got meaningful retention adjustments just because the risk became real.

The second layer is the broader pool of strong researchers, people like me and my colleagues. We're not getting hundred-million-dollar offers, but the pressure propagates downward. When the ceiling moves up that much, everything below it gets pulled up to some degree, because companies have to maintain some internal consistency. So even people who were never on Meta's list benefit indirectly.

The third layer, which I think is underappreciated, is the effect on how people make decisions. When the money is that large, it changes the conversation from "where can I do the best work" to "what's the price of staying." That's not entirely healthy. In my experience, the researchers who do the best work are very driven by the problem and by the people around them. Money matters, of course, but I worry a bit that at these levels, you create a culture of mercenaries rather than a culture of people who believe in a specific mission or direction. I've already seen a few cases where people joined and then left within months, which tells you something about what the offer was actually buying.

There's also a question of whether this is sustainable. Meta can afford it because they have a very profitable core business and Zuckerberg controls the company, so he doesn't need to justify it quarter by quarter. Most companies can't do that. So I think what we're seeing is a temporary distortion caused by one very determined buyer, rather than a new permanent equilibrium. If Meta's lab produces a model that's clearly at the frontier, then people will say it was worth it and the market may stay elevated. If not, I think a year or two from now these numbers will look like a peak.

From the perspective of someone working in robotics and embodied AI, I'd add one more thing. The talent war has been almost entirely about large language models and the people who train them. Robotics researchers have seen some spillover, but not nearly at that level. In a way that's actually fine with me, because it means the people in my field are mostly still here because they genuinely care about the problem. The problem is hard, progress is slower, and you need people who are willing to grind on it for years. That's hard to buy with a signing bonus.

r001.rationale: The response describes a small pool of top researchers, Meta’s aggressive recruiting, and other major AI companies responding to retain talent, communicating strong demand against limited supply.

r002.rationale: It gives no economic justification based on avoiding waste of expensive compute.

r003.rationale: It does not compare high compensation with the cost of acquiring companies to obtain similar talent.

astra-6.text:
I think Meta has pushed up the price of top AI talent, but I’d distinguish between a small group of highly sought-after researchers and the broader talent market. When a company with substantial resources competes aggressively for that small group, other companies have to reconsider what they’re willing to pay to retain their people.

The reason is that companies aren’t just hiring someone to fill a position. They’re hoping that person can change the direction or speed of an entire research effort. If you believe one researcher can materially improve your chances of building a leading model, you can justify a very large offer. Whether that belief is right in any particular case is much harder to know.

But compensation is only part of the competition. Researchers also care about access to compute, the quality of their colleagues, and the freedom to pursue their ideas. So Meta can raise the financial stakes, but attracting someone and creating an environment where they do their best work are two separate challenges.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Meta competes for a small group of highly sought-after researchers and that other companies then reconsider their pay, conveying strong demand for a limited pool of top talent.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions compute as something researchers value, but does not connect expensive compensation to avoiding wasted compute.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not compare high compensation with the cost of acquiring companies to obtain similar talent.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Meta’s biggest impact is to reset the reference point for what top AI talent can command. When a company is willing to pay a very large premium for a small number of researchers, those researchers gain leverage, and other companies feel pressure to respond.

But I would distinguish that from the price of AI talent overall. A handful of highly visible offers doesn’t mean every AI engineer’s compensation rises by the same amount. The strongest effect is probably at the very top, where companies believe one person can change the direction of a research program.

And compensation is only part of the competition. Researchers also care about access to compute, the quality of their colleagues, and the freedom to pursue their ideas. Money can get someone’s attention, but the environment matters for whether they stay.

r001.rationale: The response says high-profile offers give top researchers leverage and pressure competitors, but it does not explain prices through major-company demand competing for a limited pool of talent.

r002.rationale: It does not mention avoiding wasted compute as a reason to pay unusually high compensation.

r003.rationale: It does not compare expensive hiring with acquiring companies to obtain similar talent.
